earlier_scan.source_named: Stevenson, Roland C. (1956-57) A survey of the phonetics and grammatical structure of the Nuba Mountain languages (Afrika und Uebersee), covering Heiban/Ebang; also Schadeberg (1981) A Survey of Kordofanian

new_statements.quote: Prosodies: Tone (High, Mid, Low), Vowel Length and Dipthongs. Stevenson notes that in most Kordofanian languages "dynamic stress accompanied by High or Low tone plays a greater role than syllabic pitch as such ..." (Tucker and Bryan 1956:272). In Heiban, lexical tone appears to be prominent as shown by the following examples. [gárò 'vegetable' (like Arabic ajur), gàrò 'grunt' (sound of a pig), gárɔ́ 'grass', ... ŋulaŋ 'seed' versus ŋulaŋ 'implement used for planting'] Rising and falling tones are also noted in long vowel endings e.g. lìrkò 'knee' versus lìrkɔ̂: 'a cabbage-like plant whose seeds only are used.' [fn. 2: Tone is marked as follows: High [´], Mid [¯], Low [`]]
new_statements.citation: Kihore, Yared Magori. 1978. A comparative study of the noun-class systems of Heiban and Kiswahili. MA thesis, University of Khartoum, Institute of African and Asian Studies, Dept of Sudanese and African Languages. Sec. 1.1.1 'Phonology of Heiban'.
new_statements.locator: p. 2 (thesis pagination; PDF p. 11), sec. 1.1.1 Phonology of Heiban, plus footnote 2
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ebang/Heiban is described as a lexical tone language with three level tones (High, Mid, Low) plus rising and falling tones on long final vowels, shown by minimal pairs. The only statement about stress is second-hand and generic: Stevenson (as reported by Tucker & Bryan 1956:272) holds that in most Kordofanian languages a dynamic stress accompanied by high or low tone matters more than syllabic pitch as such. No rule for where stress falls in the word is given by any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author says tone 'appears to be' prominent and gives no full tonal or accentual analysis. Meinhof 1943/44:95 reports the contrary second-hand opinion of K. G. Nobbs that musical tone plays no role in Heiban (it does in Tira).
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation-form nouns from Khartoum informants (Pastor Adam Kuku Kafi and two others); word level only. Kihore's bibliography lists Tucker & Bryan as the 1966 'Linguistic Analyses' volume while the in-text citation says 1956:272; the quoted stress sentence is Stevenson's generalisation about Kordofanian, not an Ebang-specific placement statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Kihore 1978 calls the language 'Heiban' (Koalib-Moro group); his informants were Heiban speakers in Khartoum/Omdurman (Pastor Adam Kuku Kafi, Yagoub Mubarak, Mohamed Abd-el-Rahman); Guest 1997 says Adam Kuku Kafi is of the Abul tribe, so Kihore's data may be Abul-dialect Ebang (Glottolog treats Abul as an alternative name under heib1243, no separate code). Meinhof 1943/44 describes the 1931 Gospel translations' 'Heiban (auch Ebaŋ genannt)', i.e. the Heiban dialect proper.

sources.note: Sec. 1.1.1 'Phonology of Heiban', p. 2 (PDF p. 11): prosodies = tone (High, Mid, Low), vowel length, diphthongs; quotes Stevenson (via Tucker & Bryan 1956:272) that in most Kordofanian languages 'dynamic stress accompanied by High or Low tone plays a greater role than syllabic pitch as such', then states 'In Heiban, lexical tone appears to be prominent' with H/M/L minimal pairs and rising/falling tones on long final vowels. No stress-placement rule. Scan via Wayback of rogerblench.info (Blench's Heiban page, 'unpublished data from Elizabeth Guest and others').

sources.note: 'A. Lautbestand' p. 96 gives consonant and vowel inventories only, following the Rejaf orthography of the 1931 Gospels; Meinhof writes 'Ich selbst habe die Sprache nicht gehört'. p. 95 passes on K. G. Nobbs' remark: 'Nach Nobbs spielt der musikalische Ton keine Rolle im Heiban, wohl aber im Tira.'
